title: Describing things
goal: Change adjectives to match the noun they describe — only three forms — and master the habit that trips up beginners: marking definiteness twice at once.
bekal: use the base form, the *-t* form and the *-e* form
build *den store bilen* with three markers at once
recognize adjectives that refuse to add *-t*
wave: Review **unit 10** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English, and rebuild the dialogue. Just one question: when *sin*, when *hans*?

dialogs.title: Dialogue — På hittegodskontoret
dialogs.intro: The lost-and-found office at the station. Budi lost his backpack on the tram two days ago, and the clerk behind the counter looks like he has heard this story a thousand times.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Den er stor og grønn. En gammel sekk.
lines.id: It's big and green. An old backpack.
lines.literal: it is big and green. an old backpack.

lines.speaker: Betjenten:
lines.text: Vi har mange grønne sekker. Hva var inni?
lines.id: We have lots of green backpacks. What's inside?
lines.literal: we have many green backpacks. what is inside?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ei blå bok, et lite håndkle og en rød lue.
lines.id: A blue book, a small towel and a red hat.
lines.literal: a blue book, a small towel and a red hat.

lines.speaker: Betjenten:
lines.text: Den store, grønne sekken med den røde lua… vent litt.
lines.id: The big green backpack with the red hat… wait a moment.
lines.literal: the big, green backpack-the with the red hat-the… wait a-little.

lines.speaker: Betjenten:
lines.text: Vi har tre. En gammel, en ny og en veldig skitten.
lines.id: We have three. One old, one new and one very dirty.
lines.literal: we have three. one old, one new and one very dirty.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: The old one is probably mine.

lines.speaker: Betjenten:
lines.id: Is the book thick or thin?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Veldig tykk. Det er ei norsk grammatikkbok.
lines.id: Very thick. A Norwegian grammar book.
lines.literal: very thick. it is a Norwegian grammar-book.

lines.speaker: Betjenten:
lines.text: Da er det din. Ingen andre mister slike bøker med glede.
lines.id: Then it's yours. Nobody else would be happy to lose a book like that.
lines.literal: then is it yours. nobody else loses such books with pleasure.

notes: **Norwegian adjectives have only three forms**, and the third doubles as the plural: *stor* (base), *stort* (for *et*-words), *store* (plural and after a definite marker). Compare German with its sixteen possibilities; Norwegian offers three.

**Et lite håndkle** breaks the rule: the *et*-word form of *liten* is not *litet* but **lite**. *Liten* is the only truly irregular adjective in Norwegian — and it's used a lot, so learn it now: *liten, lita, lite, små*.

**Den store, grønne sekken** uses **three definite markers at once**: *den* in front, the *-e* ending on every adjective, and the *-en* ending on the noun. This is called double definiteness, and Norwegian is one of the few languages that does it. English makes do with a single "the".
**Danish and Swedish differ here.** Danish drops the ending (*den store sæk*), Swedish keeps it (*den stora säcken*). If you've touched either one, don't carry the habit over.

**Den gamle er nok min** — an adjective can stand alone without a noun when the thing is clear from the conversation. *Den gamle* = "the old one". English needs "one"; Norwegian doesn't. This shortcut is used all the time.

**Ei norsk grammatikkbok** — the adjective *norsk* doesn't change even though the noun is an *ei*-word. Adjectives that already end in *-sk*, *-ig* or *-t* never add another *-t*. The list is on the next page.

grammars.title: The three adjective forms
body: Two things decide the form: the gender of the noun, and whether the noun is definite or not.

head: Situation
Form
Example
English
rows: the car is big; the house is big

after: The last row matters: when an adjective stands after *er* or *blir*, it never takes *-e*, even if the noun is definite. *Bilen er stor*, not *bilen er store*.
But if the noun is plural, it still takes *-e* in this position: *bilene er stor**e***. So *-e* marks plural **and** definiteness; *-t* marks neuter gender.

grammars.title: Double definiteness
body: This pattern is a Norwegian trademark. Read the three parts as one sound, not three separate pieces.
after: ⚠️ When there is **no** adjective, the demonstrative is dropped: *bilen* already means "the car". *Den* is only required when an adjective comes in between.
Every adjective in a row takes *-e*, not just the first: *den nye, røde genseren*.

One group drops the noun ending even with an adjective: names and family relations that are already definite — *min gamle venn*, *hele dagen*, *neste uke*. The words *hele*, *neste*, *forrige* and *samme* are always followed by a noun without an ending.

grammars.title: Rebellious adjectives
body: The only part you have to memorize. Everything else follows the three forms above without arguing.

head: Group
What happens
Example
rows: et hyggel**ig** hus, et vikt**ig** møte
et nor**sk** hus, et indonesi**sk** ord
et sv**art** bord, et lett spørsmål
et mod**erne** hus, et stille rom
et bl**ått** hus, et gr**ått** hus, et n**ytt** hus

after: *Liten* has five forms and all of them are common: *en liten gutt*, *ei lita jente*, *et lite hus*, *små barn*, *den lille gutten*. The last one — **lille** after a demonstrative — is the one most often forgotten.
Adjectives ending in *-el*, *-en*, *-er* drop the middle *e* when adding *-e*: *gammel → gamle*, *sulten → sultne*, *vakker → vakre*.

blocks.text: Notice that *skitten* is pronounced **SHIHT-ten** — *sk* before *i* sounds like *sh*, as set out on the pronunciation page. And *morsom* sounds like **MOO-som**: the first *o* becomes "oo", the second stays "o".

sections.title: Eye training: one adjective, six situations

blocks.text: Read each row aloud from left to right in one breath.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Describe five things around you with two adjectives each, in indefinite and definite form: *en stor, grønn sekk → den store, grønne sekken*.
If you stumble, the cause is almost always the same: you forgot the noun's gender. The adjective rules themselves are very short; what takes memory is the *en/ei/et*.
Say all five forms of *liten* in one go — *liten, lita, lite, lille, små* — until it flows. It's the only adjective truly worth memorizing on its own.
